message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Here's everything, in the order you asked.

## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the edge of the tile next to it.** You can see it when light skims across the floor, and you can feel it in socks. It also catches dirt and can be a trip hazard.

It usually comes from an uneven floor, uneven adhesive, or long tiles like yours having a very slight natural curve. Two things help a lot:
- **Tile levelling clips:** cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.
- **A one-third offset:** if you stagger the tiles in a brick pattern, shift each row by a third of a tile rather than half. With 60 cm tiles, a half-tile offset makes any curve line up at the worst point.

## Grout colour

For pale grey porcelain, go for **a mid-grey, or a grey a shade or two darker than the tile**. It hides everyday dirt, and because it's in the same colour family, the floor looks calm rather than gridded. Avoid white or very pale grout on a floor, because that's the one that looks grubby within weeks.

Two practical points:
- Grout often dries a different shade from how it looks wet or on the bag. If you can, grout a couple of spare tiles as a test board first.
- A **stain-resistant grout**, or sealing a standard cement grout, makes a real difference on a bathroom floor.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Before.** Tiling right across and setting the toilet on the finished floor avoids fiddly cuts around the base, gives a cleaner seal, and means the toilet can be replaced later without leaving a gap in the tiling.

One check: the tiles and adhesive will raise the floor by roughly 1 to 1.5 cm. Make sure the toilet's waste connection still lines up at the new height.

## How many boxes

**Buy 4 boxes.** Here's the working:

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 m × 1.8 m | 4.32 m² |
| Area per tile | 0.3 m × 0.6 m | 0.18 m² |
| Tiles to cover the floor | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 | 24 tiles |
| Add 10% | 24 × 1.1 = 26.4, rounded up | 27 tiles |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, rounded up | **4 boxes** (32 tiles) |

Three boxes would be exactly 24 tiles with nothing to spare. That's not enough once you make cuts, break one (everyone does), or find the walls aren't perfectly square. Four boxes leaves you 8 spare.

That's more than 10%, which is no bad thing for a first floor with a brick pattern and cuts around the toilet. Whatever you don't use, keep a couple of tiles for future repairs.

Check that all four boxes have the **same batch number**, because the shade can vary slightly between batches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [names],
>
> Just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor this Saturday morning, roughly [9am to 12pm], so there'll be some noise from the cutter. I'll try to get the cutting done in one go to keep it as short as possible.
>
> Thank you for being so patient with the skip on the drive these last two weeks. It should be gone soon. We really appreciate it.
>
> [Your names]

## Three tips for your first floor

1. **Spend most of your effort on the floor underneath.** It needs to be solid, clean and flat. Check it with a long straight edge. A timber floor that flexes needs overboarding with tile backer board before tiling, and the right primer for your surface matters too. Most failed tiling jobs come down to the floor underneath, not the tiling itself.

2. **Lay the tiles out dry before you mix anything.** Arrange them on the floor to plan where the cuts fall. Start from the doorway or the most visible line, and avoid thin slivers against walls. Leave a small gap at the walls for expansion; the skirting will cover it.

3. **Work in small batches and check your coverage.** Mix only as much adhesive as you can use before it skins over. For tiles this size, spread adhesive on the back of each tile as well as the floor. After laying the first few, lift one to check it's fully covered underneath. Then don't walk on the floor for at least 24 hours, or whatever your adhesive specifies.

You're right that the videos make it look easy. Those people have done it hundreds of times. Going slowly and checking as you go matters more than speed, and a 2.4 × 1.8 m room is a sensible size for a first floor. Good luck.
